Sample Size for AIPE on a Partial Correlation

Source: R/ss_aipe_partial_r.R
ss_aipe_partial_r.Rd

Takes a planning value of the population partial correlation \(\rho_{XY \cdot Z_1 \cdots Z_{p-1}}\), the number of predictors (X and the variables partialed out), and a desired confidence interval width, and returns the smallest sample size at which the interval is expected to be that narrow (accuracy in parameter estimation, AIPE; Kelley, 2008). With assurance it returns the smallest sample size at which the realized interval is that narrow with at least the stated probability.

Usage

ss_aipe_partial_r(
  true_cor,
  p,
  width,
  which_width = c("Full", "Lower", "Upper"),
  conf_level = 0.95,
  fisher_z = FALSE,
  assurance = NULL
)

Arguments

true_cor

Population partial correlation \(\rho_{XY \cdot Z_1 \cdots Z_{p-1}}\) (written \(\rho\) in Details) the sample size is planned for, in \((-1, 1)\). The planner treats this value as the truth; ss_aipe_partial_r_sensitivity shows what the plan delivers when the truth (true_cor there) differs from the value planned with (supposed_cor there).

p

Number of predictors in the regression of Y on X and the variables partialed out, so p - 1 variables are partialed out and p is at least 2. A categorical variable with a levels counts as a - 1 predictors. It is the p of ss_power_R2, ci_R2, and ci_reg_coef: the correlation concerns one predictor of a regression with p predictors. In the notation of a model comparison, \(q\) is the number of predictors removed from the full model to give the restricted model (\(q = p_{full} - p_{restricted}\), the predictors being tested), and the number of variables partialed out is \(p - q\); this correlation concerns one predictor, so \(q = 1\) and \(p - 1\) variables are partialed out.

width

Desired full width of the confidence interval on the partial correlation.

which_width

Whether width is the "Full" width of the interval (default) or a half-width: "Lower" and "Upper" both interpret width as half the full width, so they plan for a full width of twice width and return the same sample size. Because the interval is not generally symmetric about the estimate (with fisher_z = TRUE in particular), its realized lower and upper half-widths can differ from each other and from half the full width; the planner does not target them separately. A genuinely one-sided width target is not currently offered.

conf_level

Desired confidence level (default 0.95).

fisher_z

Logical. If TRUE, the plan is for the interval formed on Fisher's Z scale (variance \(1/(N - p - 2)\)) and back-transformed with \(\tanh\). If FALSE (default), the plan is for the interval formed on the raw scale from the first-order variance.

assurance

Optional. The probability that the realized interval is no wider than width. The function returns the smallest sample size, at or above the sample size planned without it, at which that probability is at least assurance. A single number above 0.5 and below 1; when NULL (the default) the plan is for the expected width only.

Value

A data.frame with the columns term and value and one row per term:

necessary_N

the planned total sample size.

expected_width

the full width of the interval at necessary_N when the sample partial correlation equals true_cor.

true_cor, p, width, conf_level

the inputs, with width the width as given.

assurance

the requested probability; present only when assurance was given.

assurance_attained

the probability, at necessary_N and true_cor, that the realized interval is no wider than the target; present only when assurance was given. It is at least assurance and exceeds it because the sample size is a whole number.

Details

Estimand and interval. The quantity planned for is the population partial correlation between \(X\) and \(Y\) given \(Z_1, \ldots, Z_{p-1}\), for independent observations from a multivariate normal population. The interval is two-sided at conf_level and is one of two Wald intervals, chosen by fisher_z; the plan is for the one chosen, and a study that reports the other is not the study that was planned. Below, \(\rho\) is that partial correlation (true_cor) and \(1 - \alpha\) is conf_level.

Raw scale, first-order variance (fisher_z = FALSE). The first-order variance of a simple correlation is \((1 - \rho^2)^2 / N\) (Olkin & Finn, 1995, Equation 3). The sample partial correlation given \(p - 1\) variables is distributed as a simple correlation from \(N - (p - 1)\) observations (Fisher, 1924, p. 330, for normally distributed variables), and the functions here use \((1 - \rho^2)^2 / (N - p)\), which differs from that at order \(1/N^2\) (see var_partial_r). The interval is \(r \pm z_{1 - \alpha/2} (1 - r^2) / \sqrt{N - p}\), with half-width $$w_{1/2}(r, N) \;=\; z_{1 - \alpha/2}\, \frac{1 - r^2}{\sqrt{N - p}}.$$ Setting \(r = \rho\) and solving for the smallest whole \(N\) with \(w_{1/2} \le\) the target half-width gives $$N \;=\; p + \Big\lceil z_{1 - \alpha/2}^2 \, (1 - \rho^2)^2 / w_{1/2}^{2} \Big\rceil.$$

Fisher's Z scale (fisher_z = TRUE). Bonett and Wright (2000, Section 3, pp. 24–25) plan the sample size for a simple correlation so that the interval formed on Fisher's Z scale (Fisher, 1921, 1924) and back-transformed has the desired width. The same plan is applied here to the partial correlation, with the standard error \(1/\sqrt{N - p - 2}\) in place of \(1/\sqrt{N - 3}\). With \(Z = \mathrm{arctanh}(r)\) and standard error \(1/\sqrt{N - p - 2}\), the interval is \(\tanh(Z \pm z_{1 - \alpha/2} / \sqrt{N - p - 2})\), and half its width is $$w_{1/2}(r, N) \;=\; \tfrac{1}{2}\Big\{ \tanh\!\Big(\mathrm{arctanh}(r) + \frac{z_{1 - \alpha/2}}{\sqrt{N - p - 2}}\Big) - \tanh\!\Big(\mathrm{arctanh}(r) - \frac{z_{1 - \alpha/2}}{\sqrt{N - p - 2}}\Big) \Big\}.$$ The planner finds the smallest \(N\) of at least \(p + 3\) at which this is no larger than the target at \(r = \rho\), by a one-dimensional search (the half-width decreases in \(N\)). This interval stays inside \((-1, 1)\) and is generally the more accurate of the two when \(N - p\) is small or \(|\rho|\) is large.

The assurance step. A plan without assurance makes the interval as narrow as the target when the sample partial correlation equals true_cor; in about half of all samples it is wider. With assurance the function finds the sample size at which the realized interval is no wider than the target with at least that probability, from the sampling distribution of the sample partial correlation:

  1. At a given \(N\) the width of either interval depends on the sample only through \(r\), and both half-widths above decrease as \(|r|\) grows. The realized interval is therefore no wider than the target exactly when \(|r| \ge r^*(N)\), where \(r^*(N)\) is the \(|r|\) at which the half-width equals the target half-width \(h\): on the raw scale \(r^*(N) = \sqrt{1 - h \sqrt{N - p} / z_{1 - \alpha/2}}\), and on Fisher's scale the root of \(w_{1/2}(r, N) = h\). When the half-width at \(r = 0\), the widest the interval can be, already meets the target, every sample does and the probability is 1.

  2. Under multivariate normality the sample partial correlation given \(p - 1\) variables from \(N\) observations is distributed as a simple correlation from \(m = N - (p - 1)\) observations. Its distribution function is computed as $$F(c) \;=\; \int_0^1 T_{2m - 3}\!\Big(\sqrt{2m - 3}\, \Big\{\frac{c\,\sqrt{1 - b}}{\sqrt{1 - c^2}} - \frac{\rho\,\sqrt{b}}{\sqrt{1 - \rho^2}}\Big\}\Big)\, g(b)\, db,$$ where \(T_{2m - 3}\) is the distribution function of Student's t on \(2m - 3\) degrees of freedom and \(g\) is the density of the beta distribution with parameters \((m - 1)/2\) and \((m - 2)/2\). The form follows from writing \(r / \sqrt{1 - r^2}\) as \((Z + \theta \sqrt{U}) / \sqrt{V}\), with \(Z\) standard normal, \(U\) and \(V\) chi square on \(m - 1\) and \(m - 2\) degrees of freedom, all independent, and \(\theta = \rho / \sqrt{1 - \rho^2}\), and then conditioning on \(U / (U + V)\). It uses the central t only, because R's noncentral t is an approximation at the noncentrality values that plans for narrow intervals reach.

  3. The probability at \(N\) is \(P_N = 1 - F(r^*(N)) + F(-r^*(N))\).

  4. The function returns the smallest \(N\), at or above the sample size planned without assurance, with \(P_N \ge\) assurance, found by doubling a step upward and then bisecting. assurance_attained is \(P_N\) at that \(N\).

The probability is exact, up to numerical integration, under multivariate normality for the interval that is planned. It was checked by simulation in two ways: in 112 planning sets of 200,000 simulated correlations each, the proportion of intervals no wider than the target at the planned sample size was within .0023 of \(P_N\); and in 16 further planning sets simulated from regression data (20,000 data sets each, with the variables partialed out by least squares) it was within .004 of \(P_N\), about two Monte Carlo standard errors, and between .002 and .012 above the request.

Four properties of the step are worth knowing.

  • The answer is never below the sample size planned without assurance. Below that sample size \(P_N\) is not monotone in \(N\) (at a very small \(N\) the sample correlation is variable enough to exceed \(r^*(N)\) by chance, and does so less often as \(N\) grows, before the narrowing of the interval takes over), so a smaller \(N\) that happens to meet the request is not a plan. At or above it \(P_N\) did not decrease in any of 72 planning sets scanned over every whole \(N\).

  • When true_cor is 0 the plan without assurance already makes the interval as narrow as the target in every sample, since the interval is widest at \(r = 0\); assurance then adds nothing and assurance_attained is 1. Near 0 the same holds approximately and the step adds little.

  • As \(|\rho|\) grows the width becomes more variable from sample to sample and the step adds more: for a width of .10 with one variable partialed out and an assurance of .80, the plan moves from 867 to 915 at \(\rho = .50\) and from 121 to 151 at \(\rho = .85\).

  • assurance must be above 0.5 and below 1; other values are refused.

Why the step is not a chi square factor. Multiplying the sample size planned without assurance by a chi square quantile over its degrees of freedom is the assurance step for an interval whose width is proportional to a sample standard deviation (Kelley & Maxwell, 2003); the width of an interval for a correlation depends on the sample through \(r\) instead, and the factor gives too few cases when \(|\rho|\) is large and too many when it is small. For one variable partialed out (\(p = 2\)), a width of .10, and a requested .80 it gives 426 at \(\rho = .70\), where the probability is .675 (448 are needed), and 1318 at \(\rho = .30\), where 1310 suffice; in the 16 planning sets simulated from regression data its sample sizes delivered from .14 below the request to .15 above it.

When to use partial or simple correlation planning. Use this function when the target is the population correlation between \(X\) and \(Y\) after statistically controlling for \(Z_1, \ldots, Z_{p-1}\). For the simple Pearson correlation, see ss_aipe_r. ss_aipe_partial_r_sensitivity simulates the plan, including under a population value other than the planning value.

References

Algina, J., & Olejnik, S. (2003). Sample size tables for correlation analysis with applications in partial correlation and multiple regression analysis. Multivariate Behavioral Research, 38(3), 309–323. doi:10.1207/s15327906mbr3803_02

Bonett, D. G., & Wright, T. A. (2000). Sample size requirements for estimating Pearson, Kendall and Spearman correlations. Psychometrika, 65(1), 23–28. doi:10.1007/BF02294183

Fisher, R. A. (1921). On the "probable error" of a coefficient of correlation deduced from a small sample. Metron, 1, 3–32.

Fisher, R. A. (1924). The distribution of the partial correlation coefficient. Metron, 3, 329–332.

Kelley, K. (2008). Sample size planning for the squared multiple correlation coefficient: Accuracy in parameter estimation via narrow confidence intervals. Multivariate Behavioral Research, 43(4), 524–555. doi:10.1080/00273170802490632

Kelley, K., & Maxwell, S. E. (2003). Sample size for multiple regression: Obtaining regression coefficients that are accurate, not simply significant. Psychological Methods, 8(3), 305–321. doi:10.1037/1082-989X.8.3.305

Maxwell, S. E., Delaney, H. D., & Kelley, K. (2027). Designing experiments and analyzing data: A model comparison perspective (4th ed.). Routledge. (See Chapter 3 on the one-way ANOVA and Chapter 4 on contrasts.)

Olkin, I., & Finn, J. D. (1995). Correlations redux. Psychological Bulletin, 118(1), 155–164. doi:10.1037/0033-2909.118.1.155

Examples

# 1. Plan N so the 95% CI on rho_XY.Z (two variables partialed out, so
#        p = 3 predictors) has full width <= 0.20, when the planning
#        value of the partial correlation is 0.30.
ss_aipe_partial_r(true_cor = 0.30, p = 3, width = 0.20)
#>  term           value
#>  necessary_N    322  
#>  expected_width 0.200
#>  true_cor       0.300
#>  p              3    
#>  width          0.200
#>  conf_level     0.950
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%

# 2. The same problem for the interval formed on Fisher's Z scale
#        (Bonett & Wright, 2000).
ss_aipe_partial_r(true_cor = 0.30, p = 3, width = 0.20, fisher_z = TRUE)
#>  term           value
#>  necessary_N    322  
#>  expected_width 0.200
#>  true_cor       0.300
#>  p              3    
#>  width          0.200
#>  conf_level     0.950
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%

# 3. With an assurance of .80: the smallest N at which the realized
#        interval is no wider than 0.20 with probability at least .80.
#        The last row is the probability at the returned N.
ss_aipe_partial_r(true_cor = 0.30, p = 3, width = 0.20, assurance = 0.80)
#>  term               value
#>  necessary_N        338  
#>  expected_width     0.195
#>  true_cor           0.300
#>  p                  3    
#>  width              0.200
#>  conf_level         0.950
#>  assurance          0.800
#>  assurance_attained 0.804
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%

# 4. A larger correlation needs fewer cases for the same width, and
#        the assurance step adds proportionally more of them.
ss_aipe_partial_r(true_cor = 0.70, p = 3, width = 0.20)
#>  term           value
#>  necessary_N    103  
#>  expected_width 0.200
#>  true_cor       0.700
#>  p              3    
#>  width          0.200
#>  conf_level     0.950
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%
ss_aipe_partial_r(true_cor = 0.70, p = 3, width = 0.20, assurance = 0.80)
#>  term               value
#>  necessary_N        126  
#>  expected_width     0.180
#>  true_cor           0.700
#>  p                  3    
#>  width              0.200
#>  conf_level         0.950
#>  assurance          0.800
#>  assurance_attained 0.809
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%
